title: How to Build a Software Engineering Portfolio
summary: Creating a portfolio as a software engineer is key to standing out as a candidate. Learn how to build one that showcases your skills and projects.
body_markdown:
- [Intuit Blog](https://www.intuit.com/blog) - [All Posts](https://www.intuit.com/blog/all-posts/) - [Social Responsibility](https://www.intuit.com/blog/hub/social-responsibility/) - [Job Readiness](https://www.intuit.com/blog/hub/job-readiness/) - How to Build a Software Engineering Portfolio A resume tells hiring teams what you know. A software engineer portfolio shows them what you can build. It doesn’t matter if you’re breaking into the industry or pivoting from a totally different career. Your portfolio is where your projects and problem-solving skills come to life. [Becoming a software engineer](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/how-to-become-a-software-engineer/) is all about proving you can bridge the gap between theory and real-world code. This guide walks you through picking your best work and organizing it into a site that actually gets you hired. ## **Key Points** - A software engineer portfolio proves what a resume can only summarize. Namely, it shows how you solve problems and communicate your work. - Portfolios can help early-career developers stand out in a competitive market. HackerRank found that 74% of developers struggle to land jobs. - The strongest portfolios include a short bio, 3 to 5 standout projects, organized technical skills, and clear contact links. - Choose projects that show range and solve real problems, like a front-end app or back-end API. - Keep your portfolio updated as your skills grow. Remove your weaker early projects and refresh your tools and technologies as you gain experience. ## **Why Does a Software Engineering Portfolio Matter?** Hiring managers move fast. That leaves you with maybe a few seconds to make an impression. A dry list of tech stacks and tools likely won’t cut it. To leave your mark, you need a portfolio that gives them something they can click and explore. Think of your portfolio as the bridge between what you know and what you can do. It shows how you tackle messy problems and write clean code. It demonstrates how you think through problems. It’s also a great way to build your personal brand and show off what makes your approach unique. Early-career developers are competing in a tough market.[HackerRank’s Developer Skills Report](https://www.hackerrank.com/reports/developer-skills-report-2025) found that 74% of developers say landing a tech job is difficult, with early-career developers hit especially hard as junior hiring lags behind senior roles. A strong portfolio helps you stand out by showing proof of work. Even if you’re still exploring the nuances of a[software engineer vs. software developer](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/software-developer-vs-software-engineer/) or just gearing up for your first interview, having real work to show is what sets you apart. ## **What Should Your Software Engineering Portfolio Include?** If you’re wondering what every software engineering portfolio website should have, always err on the side of clarity. Focus on the sections that help hiring teams get a sense for your skills fast. You want to make it as easy as possible for them to see who you are, what you’ve built, and (most importantly) how to get you on their team. Here’s where to direct your efforts: ### **A Short Bio and Introduction** Think of your “About” section as the trailer for your work. You want to keep it professional, but don’t be afraid to sound like a real person. In just a few sentences, help employers get a feel for your background and what you’re learning and building. And be sure to communicate what kind of role you’re ready to tackle next. ### **Your Best Projects** Think of this section as your curated gallery. Rather than including absolutely everything you’ve ever coded, add 3 to 5 standout projects that show your strongest work. For each project, include a clear title, a short description, the technologies used, and a link to the code or a live demo. Quality definitely beats quantity here, so choose projects that show real problem-solving. ### **Skills and Technologies** This section is your technical blueprint of sorts. Whereas your projects show your skills in action, this list is for hiring managers or recruiters to quickly check specific boxes. Consider grouping your[software engineering skills](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/software-engineer-skills/) into logical categories, like the example that follows: - **Languages:** JavaScript, Python, TypeScript - **Frameworks and libraries:** React, Node.js, Django - **Databases:** PostgreSQL, MongoDB - **Tools and platforms:** AWS, Docker, Git The idea is to help hiring managers scan your profile in seconds and immediately see where you’re strongest. ### **Contact Information and Links** Make the next step simple. After all, you want the hiring managers who love your work to effortlessly reach you. Include links to your GitHub, LinkedIn, and resume. And be sure to include a professional email address or contact form, so all it takes is a seamless, single click to contact you. ## **How to Choose Projects for Your Portfolio** The best software engineer portfolio projects prove you can think, build, test, and explain your work. Choose projects that show range and solve real problems. ### **Show a Range of Skills** Don’t get stuck in a 1-tech loop. Pick projects that highlight[different layers of the software engineering stack](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/front-end-vs-back-end-vs-full-stack-developers/) so hiring teams can see the full scope of your abilities. For example, you might feature: - **Front-end:** A sleek weather app with a focus on responsive UI/UX - **Back-end:** A robust API that handles complex authentication and data security - **Full stack:** A task manager that ties everything together with a live database **

Solve Real Problems

** To really grab hiring managers’ attention, build something people would actually use. Think about tools that scratch a real itch. For example, you could build and showcase: - A budgeting app that handles currency conversion - A job application tracker with automated reminders - A small business inventory dashboard for a local shop The goal here is to show you can take a vague need and turn it into a working, polished solution. ### **Write Clear Project Descriptions** For each project, add a short summary that explains your approach to a problem and the result. For example, you might structure your descriptions like this: “I built a full-stack expense tracker to help users organize monthly spending. I used React, Node.js, and PostgreSQL, then added charts to make spending patterns easier to understand.” And don’t forget to mix in visuals and links, including screenshots, GitHub links, or live demos. ## **Where to Host Your Portfolio** As you build your software engineering portfolio, where you host your work is almost as important as the work itself. You want a platform that’s reliable and fast. Here are some go-to options: ### **GitHub Pages** [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) is free and lets you host a portfolio site directly from a repository. It’s a strong option for early-career engineers because employers can view the live site and explore the code behind it. And it can provide serious exposure. GitHub says[more than 180 million developers](https://github.com/about) use GitHub to discover, fork, and contribute to over 420 million projects. ### **Personal Website** A personal website with a custom domain gives you full control over design, structure, and branding. You can build it with React, Next.js, or simple HTML/CSS. The site itself can also become a portfolio project if you build it thoughtfully and document your process. ### **Website Builders** Website builders like Wix, Squarespace, and Webflow can help you create a polished portfolio without coding everything from scratch. They’re useful for quick setup, especially if you want to focus your time on refining project descriptions and visuals. ## **Keep Your Portfolio Updated** Learning how to build a programming portfolio doesn’t stop once your site goes live. Your portfolio should grow as your skills grow. Add new projects when they show stronger problem-solving or experience with new technologies. And remove older work that no longer reflects your current abilities. Don’t forget to keep your skills section accurate as you learn new languages and frameworks. You can also use your portfolio to build visibility. Share new projects on LinkedIn, and engage with developer communities on GitHub, Discord, Reddit, or local tech groups. The more active your work looks, the more you strengthen your personal brand. ## **Start Building Your Portfolio Today** Don’t wait for perfection before you hit publish. Your software engineer portfolio is a living document that doesn’t have to be perfect the day it goes live. Every update helps hiring teams see the impact you’re capable of making. Once your portfolio is ready to do the talking, check out[software engineering jobs](https://www.intuit.com/careers/teams/software-engineering/) at Intuit to get an idea of what’s out there. ## FAQs ### Which platforms are best for hosting a portfolio? **** GitHub Pages is a strong free option because it hosts your site directly from a repository. A personal website with a custom domain gives you more control over branding. Website builders like Wix, Squarespace, and Webflow work well if you want a polished portfolio without building every page from scratch. ### How can you start building a software engineering portfolio with little to no experience? Start with small, practical projects that solve real problems. You could build a calculator, a budget tracker, a task manager, or a simple API. Then explain what you built, which tools you used, and what you learned. As your skills grow, replace beginner projects with stronger work. ### What is the best way to present your portfolio during interviews? Choose 1 or 2 projects that match the role. Walk through the problem, your approach, the technologies used, and the final result. Be ready to explain trade-offs and challenges you worked through to get to that result. Share the live demo and GitHub link when possible, too.
